title: The Woman Who Helped Save Israel but Was Nearly Forgotten
paragraphs: The Woman Who Helped Save Israel but Was Nearly Forgotten
There are names the world remembers because they conquered kingdoms.
And there are names Heaven remembers because they chose courage when nobody was watching.

Most believers know about Moses.
They know about David.
They know about Esther standing before a king.
But hidden between the shadows of Exodus is a woman many sermons barely mention… even though an entire nation might have died without her.
Her name was Shiphrah.
And beside her stood another forgotten warrior named Puah.

Two women.
No armies.
No titles.
No throne.
Just trembling hands… and fear of God greater than fear of Pharaoh.
And sometimes that is exactly how God saves generations.
The story begins in darkness.

Israel had multiplied in Egypt. What began as favor in Joseph’s days slowly became suspicion, then oppression, then slavery. The Egyptians looked at the Hebrews and no longer saw human beings. They saw a threat.
Exodus 1:8 says:
“Now there arose a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph.”
The Hebrew phrase is deeply haunting:

וַיָּקָם מֶלֶךְ־חָדָשׁ
Vayyāqom melekh-ḥādāsh
“A new king arose.”

Not merely a political shift.
A spiritual one.
A generation rose that had no memory of God’s mercy.
And that is still happening today.

Entire cultures forget what God once did.
Families forget the prayers that built them.
Children inherit blessings they never learned to honor.
Soon Pharaoh enslaved Israel, but oppression was not enough for him. Tyranny is never satisfied. Evil always escalates.
Then came the unthinkable command.
Exodus 1:15–16 says:
“And the king of Egypt spake to the Hebrew midwives… and he said, When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women… if it be a son, then ye shall kill him.”
In Hebrew:

אִם־בֵּן הוּא וַהֲמִתֶּן אֹתוֹ
Im-ben hu va’hamitten oto
“If it is a son, you shall put him to death.”
Can you imagine hearing that?
Imagine being ordered to kill innocent babies with your own hands.
Imagine the silence after Pharaoh finished speaking.
Imagine walking home carrying the weight of that command.
Shiphrah and Puah were not warriors in armor.
They were midwives.
Women who spent their lives helping babies breathe their first breath.
Women whose hands were trained to protect life.
And now the government demanded death.
History often celebrates loud heroes.
But Scripture quietly reveals that some of the greatest acts of faith happen in hidden rooms where nobody applauds.
Exodus 1:17 changes everything:
“But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them…”
In Hebrew:

וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
Vattir’ena hamyaldot et-haElohim
“The midwives feared God.”
This is not ordinary fear.
The Hebrew word יָרֵא — yārē’ means reverence, awe, holy trembling, deep surrender.
They feared disappointing God more than dying before Pharaoh.
That is rare.
Because most people obey whoever scares them most.

Some obey culture.
Some obey government.
Some obey popularity.
Some obey money.
Some obey social pressure.
But these women obeyed God.
And because they did, babies lived.
One of those babies would eventually be Moses.
Think about that.

Before Moses parted the sea…
before he confronted Pharaoh…
before he carried the commandments…
Two forgotten women quietly protected the generation that would deliver Israel.
Sometimes the people who change history never stand on the stage.
Sometimes they simply refuse to bow.
And maybe this is why some of you feel unseen.

You pray in secret.
You fight temptation in silence.
You raise children nobody thanks you for.
You stay faithful while others compromise.
You resist darkness when nobody would know if you gave in.
Heaven sees all of it.
The world may forget your name.
God does not.
Pharaoh questioned the women after discovering Hebrew boys were still alive.
And their answer carried holy defiance.
Exodus 1:19:
“Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them.”
Some scholars debate every nuance of the statement, but the central truth remains undeniable:
They refused to cooperate with evil.
And God honored them for it.
Exodus 1:20–21 says:
“Therefore God dealt well with the midwives… and because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses.”
That phrase is deeply powerful.

וַיַּעַשׂ לָהֶם בָּתִּים
Vayya’as lahem battim
“He made for them households.”
In ancient Hebrew understanding, a “house” was not merely a building.

It meant legacy.
Lineage.
Inheritance.
Future generations.
The women who protected life received legacy from God Himself.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully personal.
Because we live in a world still ruled by Pharaoh spirits.

A world that still normalizes death.
A world that pressures people to compromise truth.
A world that rewards silence and punishes conviction.
But every generation still has its Shiphrahs and Puahs.

People who quietly refuse corruption.
People who still fear God.
People who protect innocence.
People who choose righteousness even when it costs them.
And maybe you never saw yourself as important because you are not famous.
Neither were they.
But Heaven measures significance differently.
Jesus later echoed this same upside-down Kingdom when He said in Mark 9:35:
“If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all.”
In Greek:

διάκονος πάντων
diakonos pantōn
“Servant of all.”
The Kingdom of God has always been built on hidden obedience.
Not applause.
Not virality.
Not celebrity.
Faithfulness.
There is another reason this story matters deeply.
Shiphrah and Puah remind us that ordinary believers can resist evil systems without possessing worldly power.
That matters right now.
Some Christians think they must become famous before God can use them.
But Scripture repeatedly destroys that lie.

A shepherd boy killed Goliath.
A prisoner interpreted dreams.
A widow sustained Elijah.
A carpenter’s son redeemed humanity.
And two midwives helped preserve Israel.
God specializes in using overlooked people.
Because when Heaven moves through weak vessels, nobody can steal the glory.
And maybe that is why this story grips the soul so deeply.
Because many reading this feel forgotten too.

Discarded.
Invisible.
Overlooked.
Uncelebrated.
But your obedience may be protecting people you will never fully realize on this side of eternity.

One prayer can change a bloodline.
One act of courage can preserve a family.
One refusal to compromise can save generations.
You may never know who survives because you stayed faithful.
The enemy wants believers to think hidden obedience is meaningless.
Scripture says otherwise.
Luke 16:10 says:
“He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.”
In Greek:

πιστὸς ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ
pistos en elachistō
“Faithful in the smallest thing.”
Heaven watches the hidden places.
And one day eternity will reveal what secrecy concealed.
Maybe that is why this story still burns after thousands of years.
Because deep down, we ache to know our quiet faithfulness matters.
It does.
More than you know.
And perhaps the greatest tragedy is that many believers remember Pharaoh more than the women who resisted him.
That still happens today.

Evil becomes famous.
Faithfulness becomes forgotten.
But Heaven writes history differently.
The names of empires vanish.
The names of the righteous remain.
Hebrews 6:10 says:
“For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love…”
In Greek:

οὐ γὰρ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ἐπιλαθέσθαι
ou gar adikos ho Theos epilathesthai
“God is not unjust to forget.”
Read that slowly.
God does not forget.

Not the tears.
Not the hidden battles.
Not the prayers whispered at 2AM.
Not the sacrifices nobody thanked you for.
Not the moments you chose holiness while everyone else chose compromise.
He remembers.
Shiphrah and Puah were nearly erased from popular memory.
But not from Scripture.
Not from Heaven.
Not from God.
And maybe this article found you because your soul needed that reminder.
You are not invisible to God.
Your quiet obedience still matters.
Your hidden faithfulness still echoes in eternity.
Your resistance against darkness is not wasted.
And if you are exhausted from fighting spiritually… hear this carefully:
The same God who saw two trembling midwives in Egypt still sees you now.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some of the people Heaven used most… were the ones earth almost forgot.
